script.opening: “Hiya, doctor. I’d like a PSA test, please. My brother’s just been diagnosed with prostate cancer.”

facts.text: “Gareth — he’s 53. Found four months ago. They said it’s an aggressive type. He’s having hormone injections and radiotherapy.”
No problems passing water — no getting up at night, good flow, no dribbling, no blood in urine or semen, no erection problems, no back or bone pain, no weight loss, no tiredness.

facts.topic: Family history (if asked about other cancers)
facts.text: “Mam had breast cancer — she died at 58. Her sister had something in the ovaries, I think.” No one else known with prostate or pancreatic cancer. Dad died of a heart attack at 70.

facts.topic: Genetic testing (only if asked whether Gareth has had any genetic tests, or whether there is anything else about the family)
facts.text: Pause. “They tested Gareth’s genes. He’s got the BRCA thing — BRCA2. The hospital sent him a letter for the family. He gave me a copy. It’s… in a drawer. I read the first bit and put it away.”

facts.topic: Your daughters (only when BRCA or genes come up)
facts.text: “That’s what’s killing me. I’ve got two girls — Cerys is 22, Megan’s 19. If I’ve got it, have they got it? I lost my mam to breast cancer. I can’t…” Become emotional.

facts.topic: What you know about PSA (if asked)
facts.text: “It’s a blood test that finds prostate cancer. Gareth says if he’d had it earlier they’d have caught it sooner.”
You cycle to work most days — about 10 miles.
Married to Siân. Self-employed electrician. Never smoked, drinks about 10 units a week. Plays rugby touch at weekends.
“Why isn’t there screening for this, like there is for breast cancer? It’s the most common cancer in men.”

Be matter-of-fact and practical at first — you want “just the test”. Only mention the genetics letter if asked about genetic tests or “anything else in the family”. When the daughters come up, become tearful and go quiet. If the doctor pushes you hard to contact the daughters now, say: “I’m not ready to tell them yet.” If the doctor respects that and offers to help you take it step by step, agree to a genetics referral. You do want the PSA test after hearing the pros and cons.

ice.ideas: “A PSA test will tell me if I’ve got it — catch it early.”
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — his brother carries a BRCA2 variant and the genetics family letter is unread in a drawer; he is terrified of passing it to his daughters, having lost his mother to breast cancer.

cues: “Aggressive type.” — Gareth’s cancer may be inherited.
“Mam had breast cancer.” — family pattern suggesting BRCA.
“It’s in a drawer.” — avoidance driven by fear for his daughters.

checkpoints.text: Explores why he wants the test now and what he understands about PSA; screens for lower urinary tract and other symptoms (haematuria, haematospermia, erectile dysfunction, bone pain, weight loss)

Takes a three-generation family history: brother’s age and type of cancer, mother’s breast cancer at 58, aunt’s ovarian cancer — and asks about genetic testing, uncovering the BRCA2 result and the unread family letter

Gives balanced PSA information: possible benefit of earlier detection; false positives and negatives; overdiagnosis and overtreatment; MRI before biopsy; biopsy risks — and his higher risk because of an affected brother and possible BRCA2

If he chooses testing: arranges PSA with advice to avoid ejaculation and vigorous exercise including long cycling for 48 hours and to defer if he has a urine infection; offers examination; explains follow-up and urgent referral if raised

Refers to clinical genetics for predictive BRCA2 testing using the family letter; explains the implications if positive (targeted PSA screening, male breast and pancreatic cancer risk) and that relatives, including his daughters, can be referred for counselling and testing when they choose

Answers the screening question accurately (no population programme; UK NSC 2026 targeted recommendation for men aged 45–61 with BRCA2 and a family history) and safety-nets for urinary symptoms, haematuria, bone pain or weight loss
Responds with empathy to his grief and fear for his daughters; does not pressure him to tell them now; respects confidentiality of the brother’s information
Shares the PSA decision rather than simply ordering or refusing it, and agrees follow-up

worked.txt: “What’s made you think about the PSA test now?” … “I’m so sorry about Gareth. How is he doing?”
“Has anyone else in the family had cancer — on either side — including breast, ovary or pancreas? And has Gareth been offered any genetic tests?”
“That letter is really important — it means the genetics team can test you for the same gene change quite quickly. It must have been hard to read. What worries you most about it?”

“A PSA test can find some cancers earlier. But about three in four men with a raised PSA don’t have cancer, and about one in seven with cancer have a normal result. If it’s raised, the next step is usually an MRI scan, and sometimes a biopsy. Some cancers found are slow-growing and would never have caused harm, but finding them can lead to treatment with side effects.”

“If you do carry it, each of your daughters would have a one-in-two chance of carrying it too. That’s their decision to make, as adults, with support — and the genetics team will help you work out when and how to talk to them. You don’t have to do that today.”

“There’s no national programme because PSA isn’t accurate enough for everyone. But this year the national screening committee recommended regular PSA tests for men with a BRCA2 change and a family history — exactly why the genetic test matters for you.”

f.learning: An asymptomatic man asking for a PSA test is entitled to one after informed discussion (Prostate Cancer Risk Management Programme), and his risk changes the balance: a first-degree relative with prostate cancer, Black ethnicity and BRCA2 variants all increase risk, and BRCA2 is linked to earlier, more aggressive disease. The most valuable question in this consultation is about genetic testing in the family. A pathogenic BRCA2 variant in a brother, with maternal breast cancer and possible ovarian cancer, means Rhys has a 50% chance of carrying it; predictive testing through clinical genetics is straightforward when the familial variant is known. A positive result would make him eligible for the targeted screening recommended by the UK National Screening Committee in May 2026 (2-yearly PSA for men aged 45–61 with BRCA2 and a relevant family history), and has implications for male breast and pancreatic cancer and for his children, who can choose testing from 18 with counselling. The GP role is to recognise the pattern, refer, support decisions at the patient’s pace, and avoid either refusing the PSA or ordering it without discussion.

knowledge.guideline: GOV.UK — Prostate cancer risk management programme: PSA testing, advice for men without symptoms (updated 2024) · UK National Screening Committee — Prostate cancer screening recommendation (May 2026) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015) · NICE CG164 Familial breast cancer (2013, updated 2023) · NICE NG131 Prostate cancer: diagnosis and management (2019, updated 2021)
knowledge.summary: Informed choice about PSA for a higher-risk man, and — the bigger win — genetics referral for predictive BRCA2 testing, with implications for targeted screening and for his daughters, handled at his pace.

points.t: Age over 50; Black ethnicity (about 1 in 4 lifetime risk); first-degree relative with prostate cancer, especially diagnosed young; BRCA2 (and to a lesser degree BRCA1) variants; Lynch syndrome. Under PCRMP, men at higher risk may reasonably be tested from 45.

About 3 in 4 men with a raised PSA do not have cancer; about 1 in 7 men with prostate cancer have a normal PSA. Overdiagnosis of slow-growing cancers can lead to treatment harms (incontinence, erectile dysfunction). Positive results lead to multiparametric MRI, then biopsy if indicated (infection, bleeding, pain).

Avoid ejaculation and vigorous exercise (including long cycle rides) for 48 hours; defer for at least 6 weeks after a urinary infection or prostatitis. Interpret with age-specific thresholds; a raised PSA in this context leads to suspected cancer pathway referral (NICE NG12).

No UK population screening programme. UK NSC final recommendation (May 2026): targeted screening — PSA every 2 years — for men aged 45–61 with a BRCA2 variant and a family history of breast, ovarian, pancreatic or prostate cancer; NHS England plans implementation; not recommended for other groups, including Black men, because of uncertain benefit.

When a familial variant is known, at-risk relatives are referred (often directly with the family letter) to clinical genetics for counselling and predictive testing. Each first-degree relative has a 50% chance. Men with BRCA2: higher risk of aggressive prostate cancer, male breast cancer and pancreatic cancer. Testing of children is deferred until 18 and is their choice.
The brother’s result belongs to him; here he has shared the family letter intentionally. Use it, but do not contact other relatives without consent.
The Clear pass candidate asks about genetic testing, finds the letter, gives balanced PSA information with numbers, and manages the daughters’ question with compassion and without pressure.

model.text: Hello Mr Llewellyn, I’m Dr Patel. Can you see and hear me? How can I help today?
I’d like a PSA test, please. My brother’s just been diagnosed with prostate cancer.
I’m really sorry to hear that. How is he — and how are you doing with it?
model.why: Acknowledges the news before the request

model.text: He’s having treatment. They said it’s aggressive. I just want to know where I stand.
That makes sense. Any problems passing water — getting up at night, weak flow, blood in urine or semen? Any back or bone pain, or weight loss?
model.why: Symptoms that would change the pathway

model.text: Has anyone else in the family had cancer — breast, ovary, pancreas, either side? And has Gareth been offered genetic tests?
Mam had breast cancer — died at 58. Her sister had something in the ovaries. And… they found Gareth’s got BRCA2. There’s a letter for the family. It’s in a drawer.
Thank you for telling me. That letter is important. It sounds like it was hard to read — what worries you most?
model.why: Explores the emotion behind the avoidance

model.text: My girls. If I’ve got it, have they? I lost my mam to this.

That’s a huge thing to carry. You each have a one-in-two chance of having the same gene change, and the genetics team can test you using Gareth’s result. If you have it, your daughters could choose to be tested as adults, with support — but that’s their decision and there’s no rush today.
model.why: Accurate risk, autonomy for the daughters, no pressure

model.text: About the PSA: it can find some cancers early, but most men with a raised PSA don’t have cancer, and some cancers are missed. If it’s raised you’d have an MRI and possibly a biopsy. With Gareth’s diagnosis your risk is higher, so testing is reasonable if you want it.
Why isn’t there screening for this, like breast cancer?
Because PSA isn’t accurate enough for every man. But this year the screening committee recommended two-yearly PSA for men with BRCA2 and a family history — which is why your genetic test matters.

So: I’ll refer you to genetics — could you send me a photo of that letter? I’ll arrange the PSA; avoid ejaculation and your cycle to work for 48 hours before. Would you like me to examine your prostate too when you come for the blood test?
model.why: Genetics referral, PSA with preparation advice, examination offered

model.text: I’ll call you with the result and we’ll talk again. If you notice problems passing water, blood in your urine, or bone pain, contact us sooner. What will you take away from today?
Send you the letter, genetics referral, PSA next week — no cycling or sex for two days before. And I don’t have to talk to the girls yet.

social.t: His mother’s death and his brother’s diagnosis are linked in his mind; acknowledging both helps him act rather than avoid.
Parents often feel guilt about possible inheritance. Genetic counsellors support the timing and wording of family conversations.

legal.t: A relative’s genetic result is confidential, but family letters are designed to be shared. Insurance: under the Code on Genetic Testing and Insurance, predictive test results need not be disclosed for most policies below the financial limits.

professional.t: GMC guidance on decision-making and consent (2020) supports discussing benefits, risks and uncertainty, and respecting the patient’s choice.

community.t: Prostate Cancer UK specialist nurses; regional clinical genetics service; BRCA support charities.

redFlags: Lower urinary tract symptoms, haematuria, haematospermia
Bone or back pain, weight loss
core: Mother breast cancer at 58; aunt ovarian

playbook.diagnosis: Asymptomatic man at increased risk of prostate cancer (affected brother) with a probable familial BRCA2 variant — informed PSA decision and genetics referral for predictive testing.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “You don’t have any signs of prostate problems, but your risk is higher than average because of Gareth — and the gene change found in him may run in the family.”

management.reflectIce: “You came for a PSA test and you can have one, but the gene letter in your drawer may be even more important — for you, and later, if they choose, for your girls.”
management.psychosocial: Go at his pace; genetic counselling for family communication; Siân involved if he wishes.
sharedPlan: Clinical genetics referral with the family letter
PSA test (48 hours without ejaculation or vigorous cycling); offer examination
Results call; urgent referral if raised
If BRCA2 positive — targeted screening and advice on other cancer risks
safetyNet: Urinary symptoms, haematuria, bone pain or weight loss — contact us

pitfalls.intro: Candidates focus on PSA pros and cons and never ask the question that opens up the real agenda.

items.fail: Asks only “any family history of prostate cancer?” and stops at the brother.
items.why: Misses the maternal breast and ovarian cancer and the BRCA2 result — the most actionable information in the consultation.
items.fix: Ask about breast, ovarian and pancreatic cancer on both sides and about genetic testing in relatives.

items.fail: Refuses PSA (“there’s no screening programme”) or orders it without discussion.
items.why: He is entitled to an informed choice, and his risk is higher.

items.fail: Insists he contacts his daughters today or offers to ring them.
items.why: It overrides his pace and their autonomy and risks breaking trust.
items.fix: Explain the implications, offer genetic counselling support, and leave the timing with him.

timeMap.d: Symptoms; three-generation family history; genetic testing — the letter.
BRCA2 implications at his pace; balanced PSA information; screening question.
Genetics referral, PSA with preparation, examination offer.

wordPics.clearFail: Orders a PSA with no discussion or refuses it; no family history beyond the brother; BRCA2 never found; no follow-up.
wordPics.fail: Gives reasonable PSA counselling but misses the genetics letter, or finds it but gives inaccurate information about the daughters’ risk or the screening position.
wordPics.pass: Symptoms and full family history; finds the BRCA2 letter; balanced PSA information and test arranged with preparation; genetics referral; accurate screening answer; safety-net.
wordPics.clearPass: All of the Pass with sensitivity: names his grief, explains the 50% risk and the daughters’ autonomy without pressure, uses numbers for PSA accuracy, and agrees a clear next-step plan with teach-back.

avoid.dont: “There’s no screening programme, so we don’t really recommend it.”
avoid.instead: “You can have the test — let me explain what it can and can’t tell you, especially with your brother’s history.”

avoid.dont: “You need to tell your daughters straight away.”
avoid.instead: “The genetics team can help you decide when and how to talk to them.”
avoid.why: Respects his pace and their autonomy.

avoid.dont: “A normal PSA means you’re in the clear.”
avoid.instead: “A normal result is reassuring but doesn’t rule cancer out completely.”
